headline: Judge Orders Waymo to Halt Overnight Charging in Santa Monica
deck: A preliminary injunction has forced the autonomous vehicle company to cease night operations at its local charging hubs, highlighting the growing friction between emerging technology and residential peace.
body: A local judge has delivered a significant blow to Waymo's operations in Santa Monica, ruling that the autonomous vehicle company must cease overnight charging activities at its facilities. Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Bradley S. Phillips granted a preliminary injunction against Waymo, citing concerns that the charging hubs near residential areas could constitute a 'public nuisance.' This decision mandates a pause in operations between 11 pm and 6 am, offering a measure of relief to residents who have voiced consistent complaints.

City officials and local residents have asserted that the constant flow of Waymo vehicles to and from these charging stations generates significant light and sound pollution, while also exacerbating traffic congestion. The disruption has been a persistent issue since Waymo began utilizing these side-by-side charging facilities in January 2025. This injunction stems from a public nuisance lawsuit filed by the City of Santa Monica against Waymo in November 2025, reflecting a year of escalating tensions.

“The constant ‘beep beep beep’ sound as the autonomous vehicles back out of their spaces (in their own lots) is an incessant disturbance that hinders both our tranquillity during the day and our peace during the night,” lamented Christopher Potter, a local resident whose daily life has been impacted by the operations.

The order specifically forbids Waymo from operating the charging lots located on Broadway at 12th and Euclid Streets during the late-night and early-morning hours. These particular facilities, situated in close proximity to homes, became flashpoints for community frustration. Neighbors described a relentless cycle of vehicles, particularly during times when the city would otherwise be quiet.

“At 2 am when the bars let out, that’s when [they had been] full bore. My apartment faces Broadway. The sound of the Waymos, yes, but the acceleration and deceleration sound that EVs have, makes it sounds like you have Tron outside your window. It [was] one after another!” recalled an anonymous neighbor, painting a vivid picture of the nightly disruption.

The City of Santa Monica has maintained that the well-being of its residents is paramount, pushing back against the operational demands of the burgeoning autonomous vehicle industry. This ruling underscores a growing municipal assertiveness in regulating the footprint of tech companies within urban landscapes. The injunction provides immediate respite as the legal proceedings continue to unfold.

“Our residents’ ability to sleep peacefully in their own homes is not negotiable. This ruling affirms what our neighbors have been telling us for more than a year, and it delivers relief while the case moves forward,” stated Mayor Caroline Torosis, emphasizing the city's commitment to quality of life for its citizens.

Waymo, for its part, has not accepted the ruling without challenge, having already filed an appeal against the injunction. The company had previously counter-sued the city following the initial lawsuit in November 2025, indicating a protracted legal struggle ahead. The next court hearing in this evolving case is scheduled for October 2026, suggesting that the broader issues remain far from resolved.

“I took a walk around last night, and gosh, it’s amazing. You can hear the crickets, you can hear your thoughts, it’s not a fleet of locusts descending on the neighborhood, it’s incredible,” shared Dylan Moore, reflecting on the immediate, tangible change brought about by the judge's order.

This judicial intervention in Santa Monica casts a harsh spotlight on the complex integration of autonomous vehicle technology into dense urban environments. It signals a critical precedent for how cities might assert control over the operational impacts of new technologies on residential quality of life. As Waymo continues its appeal, the ongoing legal battle will likely shape future regulations for AV companies seeking to expand their services into populated areas nationwide.
